The B&R Program – Part Three

My take is that you can learn as much about China's ideas, strategies, and orientations from B&R as you can from BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.

I know that comparing a program to an organization, a forum, or a treaty is flawed. But I'm making this point in the sense that within B&R, China's hands are free and it isn't bogged down in coordinating with multiple governments. At the same time, it has to allocate resources directly to projects. So maybe in BRICS and the SCO, there are moments of pleasantries and what you might call political flirting, but in B&R there's no room for those games. They have to genuinely lay out their decisions and policies clearly and transparently, and actually implement them.

Although it has never been officially stated outright, in my view (a personal interpretation), one of the main reasons China at one point encouraged Iran and Saudi Arabia to negotiate and clear up their grievances probably comes back to B&R. Setting aside the things that get written on paper, signed, and photographed (Iranian officials have racked up plenty of those photos with China), in practice China's largest volume of B&R cooperation in our region has been with Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Iraq. Cooperation with Iran hasn't been insignificant either. But sanctions, banking restrictions, and other considerations have made the scale of cooperation different.

The horizon China has for B&R spans several decades. And naturally, it aligns the decisions, policies, and resources it allocates with this project as much as possible.

In a way, you could call it a super-framework for economic and investment affairs.

By the way, Pakistan is also one of China's close partners in this program. Of course, beyond all that, Pakistan has a very deep relationship with China. In the media, it's usually referred to as an ironclad relationship (China doesn't throw around such terms and expressions lightly).

The last point worth paying attention to is that China insists strongly on defining its interactions — whether in B&R or in other cooperations — as a partnership, and emphasizes that it is not the type for alliance. The logic is that a partnership makes sense between two parties. But an alliance is usually formed against a third country, or assumes (or creates) a third rival.

This strategy leads China, in many instances, not to behave the way its partners expect it to.

The B&R Program – Part Two
The Chinese government launched the Belt & Road Initiative in 2013. "Belt" refers to the land route. "Road" here doesn't mean a road; it means a route — a maritime route.
The idea behind B&R is China's development of land and sea routes to the West (specifically Europe), and roughly 150 countries are involved. That is, China went and talked to countries one by one and worked out a framework with each of them regarding what kinds of cooperation it could have with them along this route.
There are two books about this, written by two Jonathans!
The first Jonathan is Jonathan Hillman, who wrote the book The Emperor's New Road (China and the Project of the Century).
The second Jonathan, Jonathan Fulton, has written a book on the ins and outs of the B&R program in the Arab world, which hasn't been published yet. But his previous writings and the book he previously wrote titled The Relationship Between China and the Persian Gulf Monarchies (which he also worked on with Routledge) show that he examines these kinds of topics very precisely and thoroughly.
If you don't have the patience to read the works of these two or similar material, talk to one of these AI services, or when you ask a question, tell it to also pay attention to B&R or what these people say in the context — that works too.

The Chinese government and today's Middle East situation – The B&R Program – Part One

It seems to me that friends who these days are looking to analyze the current situation in the Middle East and examine possible future scenarios are paying particularly close attention to Iran, America, and the role of regional players, while giving China a smaller share of attention.

Yet China's decisions in recent years have played an important role in the region – both in places where it intervened contrary to expectations, such as Iran-Saudi relations, and in places where, despite expectations, it did not intervene or intervened only very minimally.

And now that Iran's connections with the world have become more limited, a large portion of the fears and hopes of the country's policymakers and decision-makers naturally circles back to China.

The first thing that usually comes to mind is that China is almost the only buyer of Iran's oil, and from another angle, Iran is a cheap energy supplier and a source of access to mines and underground resources for China.

I feel that this view is not enough to understand China's decisions and policies, the actions it has taken in the region in recent years, the decisions it is making now, and its positions on events that will unfold in the region in the future.

My suggestion to friends who are interested in this topic is to read up a bit on China's Belt & Road program. Aside from being a fascinating subject, it opens our minds to China's way of looking at many regional and international issues.

Tonight, in a separate post, I'll write a few more sentences about this.

(Of course, I don't have any particular expertise in this subject. I've read a few books and articles out of personal curiosity. Dig around yourselves – you'll find more information.)

entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

Religious intellectual. I've said this several times before. The phrase "religious intellectual" was coined out of poor taste. We'd be better off using the term "religious new-thinker" instead.

In the realm of religion and religiosity, we're dealing with two groups of people. One group of religious people who just live their lives and have nothing to do with thought or reflection.

There's also a smaller group of religious people who think about religion and care deeply about it. For this second group, we can envision a spectrum ranging from religious old-thinkers to religious new-thinkers.

It's clear that everyone who spends their time thinking about religion and religious matters can be placed somewhere on this spectrum — no one is left out.

P.S. "Religious intellectual" was from the start a nonsensical, incorrect term — an incompatible, discordant compound. But perhaps the word "intellectual" itself needs to gradually be retired, and several alternative terms (depending on context and subject) should come into common use. In my view, this process is already taking shape in both Persian and English.

entry.title: [bamotamem] Typing practice: Andre Weil's biography is interesting. This French…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

Typing practice: Andre Weil's biography is interesting. This French mathematician, on a trip to Finland, was staying at a hotel near the Finland-Soviet border. To keep his wife from forgetting her touch-typing skills, he would sometimes read texts aloud to her and she would type them. They did this on that trip too (and in between, they would stop and enjoy the view). Apparently the host grows suspicious (why is someone gazing into the distance and telling his wife to type up his observations?). They open a spy file on Andre Weil so he'd be kept under closer watch. Around the same time, the Soviet Union also starts bombing Finland, and once again this unfortunate, nearsighted mathematician can't tell from a distance that Finnish air defenses are operating in the middle of a field. He stares and goes closer to see what's going on. They arrest him. Then they find he also has a spy file (the typing). Among his letters, one is also found addressed to a Russian friend, in which he tells him, "I'm waiting to see how you prove it" (he meant mathematical theorems, but they think it's about an operation). The night before he was supposed to be executed at dawn, he is miraculously saved. The book's translation has been published by Ney Publishing. I'll say more separately.

entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

Scoring in negotiation (from writings eighteen years ago) One of the rules of giving concessions in a negotiation is that if you give the other party a concession that you thought was valuable and appropriate, and they didn't accept it, or they agreed and then backed out, don't easily give that same concession again later (either give them less, or take more from them, and don't easily go back to the previous agreement). Otherwise, they might not appreciate the concession they receive again. Shopkeepers know this too. For example, when they say they'll give 20% off on something, they give this discount on the condition that the person accepts and buys it right there in the store. But if they say, 'Let me go take a walk and come back,' when they return, either they're told it's sold out, or they say we checked the system and the price is higher, or they say we called the store owner and he said that discount wasn't for this item. It's the same when landing projects. If you tell a client you can do something (at no extra cost) two weeks earlier than the norm, and you see they don't appreciate it and easily pass it by, take a look at your calendar and say, 'I made a mistake.' So they learn to appreciate it when they get a good concession. You might lose out in some places, but in the long run it has many benefits. This rule is followed at all levels of negotiation, from everyday transactions to equations and international relations, and it should be.
